rv.q: That uneasiness, though, is perhaps the triumph of the production.
Ultimately one can’t argue with the subtlety of the three central performances or the brutal logic of Dyer’s production.
This is a supple production, and one sensibly unhindered by momentum-spoiling props, and it gains force and focus as the noose of the second half tightens around all those who are not white men.
In the end, the cascade of arresting visuals wins you over.
Rosy McEwen is brave, upright, her own woman – and movingly embodies absolute trust right up to the end.
This is a slick, strongly visual yet oddly cold Othello. Fashion trumps sentiment and the verse-speaking is patchy.
This version is hot on relevance but it’s never ravishing.
His austere staging is bold in its reframing of the play’s themes, but sometimes stilted in execution.

Yes, it’s a fleet, clear, potent three-hour affair that makes welcome strides for diversity, but it stumbles in some areas, and the festive scheduling (aside from ticket prices that have you mourning the Travelex era) feels like a misstep too.
It's an intense collapse, riding Shakespeare's language to find his own meanings, an extraordinary performance at the heart of a revelatory and relevant production.
His directorial focus is forensic, magnifying the psychodrama at the heart of Shakespeare's play and turning Othello's cognitive turmoil inside out with surgical precision.
Clint Dyer delivers a powerful production with performances both dignified and passionate.

Bringing it into the twenty-first century should work but although the costumes and the setting are contemporary, they still use knives, cudgels and carry flaming torches which is anachronistic and a little confusing.

Playing at three hours long, this Othello does drag in places and for all the lights, torches and a rumbling sound design that add plenty of atmosphere to Dyer’s dystopia, there’s a nagging sense that this production is more style than substance.
This Is a laudably ambitious production, but one that has jettisoned some of the play's key emotional ballast.
Despite its shortcomings, this production would probably do great business on Broadway.
It’s intense, chilling and gripping, and crackles with such an electrifying, cinematic energy (with credit to Nina Dunn and Gino Ricardo Green for truly elemental video design).
When combined with such rich performances of psychological anguish, this production makes a centuries’-old tale feel vivid and captivating, fresh like a sharp cut.
It is a vividly atmospheric and kinetic production.

One of those productions I find more interesting to unpack than actually to watch, Dyer's take on the play is meticulously thought-out in terms of intent, but stylistically could have done with more variety of sound and vision to really push the story forward.
But it’s also a languid production which is strangely paced and which we felt could have done with a little trimming particularly as its press night is already in its rear view mirror.

cn.t: A visually bold, historically conscious production that powerfully foregrounds racism, anchored by strong performances from Terera and especially Hilton's commanding Iago, though some find it more thoughtful than emotionally seismic.
